routes.description: Establish that the existence of severe natural and moral evil does not make belief in an omnipotent, perfectly good God unreasonable when logical compatibility, human epistemic limits, theistic purposes, and the wider evidential context are considered together.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supplies a coherent basis for God and evil to coexist, blocks the inference from apparently gratuitous suffering to divine improbability, and explains why the full evidential and doctrinal context can preserve rational theistic belief.

motionBridge.description: Connect the answers to logical and evidential evil with the conclusion that theistic belief remains reasonable on the total evidence.

centralBridges.description: Show that omnipotence and perfect goodness do not logically contradict evil when significant freedom or morally sufficient permission is possible.
Show that limited human knowledge of causal consequences and providential purposes undercuts confident judgments that suffering is gratuitous.
Show how knowledge of God, freely accepted salvation, eternal life, or other divine purposes can alter the expected significance of earthly suffering.
Require the probability of God to be assessed against the whole body of relevant evidence rather than the existence of evil in isolation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how judgments that suffering is objectively evil may contribute to an affirmative moral case for a transcendent foundation.
Account for how complex contingencies could serve divine purposes while preserving meaningful creaturely freedom.

routes.description: Establish that the scale and character of suffering make belief in an almighty, all-loving, and humanly concerned deity unreasonable because proposed appeals to freedom, unknown goods, salvation, or wider evidence do not reconcile those attributes with the actual world.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if observed suffering provides a warranted adverse inference about divine goodness or power, the principal theistic defenses fail to explain a feasible better world or justify extreme harms, and secular accounts preserve moral judgment without God.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative force of natural and moral suffering with the conclusion that belief in the relevant deity is unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Show why tsunamis, childhood cancer, and comparable harms conflict evidentially with combined omnipotence, benevolence, and concern for conscious creatures.
Require an explanation of why an omnipotent God could not create significantly free creatures in a world containing substantially less natural and moral evil.
Defend ordinary moral knowledge as adequate to judge extreme suffering despite uncertainty about remote causal consequences or alleged unknown goods.
Test whether appeals to inability, permissive greater goods, salvation, and mystery jointly preserve a coherent account of divine power and goodness.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground moral obligations and humane concern in facts about sentience, needs, suffering, sympathy, and shared human experience without invoking God.
Address how religious diversity and exclusivist salvation claims affect proposed salvific explanations of indiscriminate suffering.

sections.title: Logical Compatibility, Freedom, and Better Possible Worlds
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether God and evil are logically consistent and whether significant freedom or divine feasibility can explain why a world with substantially less evil was not actualized.

sections.title: Evidential Evil, Unknown Reasons, and Human Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: This central clash determines whether apparently gratuitous suffering supports an adverse probability judgment or whether limited knowledge of consequences and divine reasons defeats that inference.

sections.title: Divine Purposes, Salvation, and Eternal Recompense
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether knowledge of God, salvation, providential purposes, and an afterlife make earthly suffering less surprising, and whether those claims adequately address severe and indiscriminate harms.

sections.title: Divine Attributes, the Actual World, and Total Evidence
sections.rationale: This section connects the character of the observed world and the wider evidential context to the motion-level question of whether belief in an omnipotent, loving, and concerned deity is reasonable.

sections.title: Objective Morality and the Foundation of Judgments About Evil
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether calling suffering objectively evil supports a transcendent moral foundation or whether natural facts about sentience, needs, and harm can ground moral obligations independently.
